Name: Sawmill Creek Loop
Summary: A gentle loop through old-growth cedar along the creek, with two footbridges and a picnic meadow at the halfway point.
Highlights: Old-growth cedar grove|Two timber footbridges|Picnic meadow|Mostly shaded
Description:
The loop starts behind the information board and follows Sawmill Creek upstream on a wide, well-drained path. The cedars here were never logged and the largest are over four metres around.

At the second footbridge the trail turns away from the water and climbs gently to a meadow with a picnic table and a view back down the valley. The return leg is a quiet forest road.

The creek is loud after rain and the first bridge can be slick. Take the loop clockwise if you want the meadow for lunch.

Name: Ridge Fire Lookout
Summary: A steady climb on an old service road to a restored fire lookout with a 360-degree view of the range.
Highlights: Restored 1938 fire lookout|Views of the whole range|Wildflowers in July|Water at the halfway spring
Description:
The service road climbs at an even grade the whole way, which makes it long rather than hard. Switchbacks begin after the spring, and the trees thin out into subalpine meadow for the last kilometre.

The lookout was restored by volunteers and is open on summer weekends. On a clear day you can see the coast to the west and the Lower Basin reservoirs to the south.

There is no shade above the spring. Start early in July and August.

Name: Twin Falls
Summary: A short, popular walk to a pair of waterfalls that are at their best in spring melt.
Highlights: Two waterfalls|Viewing platform|Benches along the way|Runs all year
Description:
This is the busiest trail in the North Fork and for good reason. The path is wide and mostly level, with a gentle final climb to a viewing platform below the upper fall.

The lower fall is a few steps off the main path on the right, about a kilometre in. It is easy to miss on the way up and worth the detour on the way back.

Spring melt is the show. In late summer the upper fall can drop to a trickle, but the pool below it stays cold and clear.

Name: Cedar Flats Boardwalk
Summary: A level boardwalk through a wetland of skunk cabbage and nurse logs. Accessible to wheelchairs and pushchairs.
Highlights: Fully accessible boardwalk|Interpretive signs|Beaver pond|Birdwatching hide
Description:
The boardwalk makes a loop through the wettest part of the valley floor. It is wide, level, and railed, and the surface is kept clear.

The hide at the far end looks across a beaver pond that fills with waterfowl in winter. Signs along the route explain how the nurse logs feed the next generation of cedar.

Mosquitoes are serious in June. Go early or go in autumn.

Name: North Fork Traverse
Trailhead: Sawmill Creek car park to Lookout Road gate
Summary: A full-day traverse linking the creek valley to the ridge, finishing at the fire lookout. Arrange a shuttle.
Highlights: Links three trails|Alpine tarn at the high point|Lookout at the finish|Shuttle required
Description:
The traverse follows Sawmill Creek to its source, climbs a rough section of trail over the headwall, and crosses the ridge to the fire lookout. The headwall is steep and loose and the route is marked by cairns rather than a path.

The high point is a small tarn that holds ice into July. From there it is downhill on good trail to the lookout and the service road.

This is the hardest day in the guide. Carry a map, start at first light, and leave a car at each end.

Name: Saddle Ridge Summit
Summary: The classic summit in the range, climbed on a well-built trail with a short scramble at the top.
Highlights: Highest point in the guide|Short Grade 1 scramble|Ptarmigan and marmots|Summit register
Description:
The trail leaves Saddle Pass through heather and climbs in long switchbacks to a shoulder below the summit block. The final hundred metres is a scramble over sound rock with good holds, exposed but never difficult.

The summit has a register in a tin box and a view of everything. Marmots live under the boulders at the shoulder and will investigate an unattended pack.

Weather changes fast here. Turn back if cloud comes over the pass.

Name: Larch Basin
Summary: A high loop through a basin of alpine larch that turns gold for two weeks in late September.
Highlights: Golden larches in late September|Three small lakes|Big views, little effort|Can be busy at peak
Description:
From the pass the trail drops briefly then climbs into the basin, where three small lakes sit among larches. The loop circles all three and returns along a bench with a view of the Saddle Ridge summit.

The larches turn in the last two weeks of September. The basin is very busy then, and the car park fills by eight. Come midweek if you can.

Snow lingers on the north side of the loop into July.

Name: Saddle Pass Meadows
Summary: An easy loop through the wildflower meadows at the pass, with benches and interpretive signs.
Highlights: Wildflowers in July|Benches with views|Interpretive signs|Good for children
Description:
The meadows loop starts at the far end of the car park and wanders through subalpine meadow on a gravel path. There is almost no climbing and plenty of places to stop.

The flowers peak in the second half of July. Lupins, paintbrush, and valerian fill the meadows and the smell carries.

Stay on the path. The meadow soil is thin and takes years to recover from a shortcut.

Name: Eastern Cirque
Summary: A long approach up Cirque Creek to a glacial cirque with a lake, a moraine, and a lot of silence.
Highlights: Glacial lake|Moraine walk|Few people|Mountain goats on the headwall
Description:
The first half follows Cirque Creek on a rough but obvious trail through avalanche slopes thick with alder. The second half climbs steeply onto the moraine and follows its crest to the lake.

The lake is milky with glacial flour and very cold. Goats are usually visible on the headwall above it, and a quiet party will see them come down to the lakeshore in the evening.

No dogs, to protect the goats. The alder can hide the trail after a wet spring.

Name: Goat Rock Viewpoint
Summary: A short, steep climb to a rock outcrop with the best view of the Saddle Ridge summit for the least effort.
Highlights: Best view-to-effort ratio in the guide|Sunset spot|Steep but short|Handrail on the final rock
Description:
The trail climbs hard from the road through open forest and reaches the outcrop in under an hour for most people. A handrail helps on the final slabs.

Goat Rock faces west, which makes it the sunset spot for the whole range. Bring a headtorch for the walk back down.

The outcrop is exposed. Keep children and dogs close at the top.

Name: Reservoir Rim Trail
Summary: A long, rolling loop around the upper reservoir with swimming beaches and a lunch shelter.
Highlights: Swimming beaches|Lunch shelter at the far end|Rolling, never steep|Open all year
Description:
The rim trail circles the upper reservoir on a mix of single track and old forestry road. It climbs and drops constantly but never for long, and there are beaches at the halfway shelter for a swim in summer.

The north shore is shaded and cool. The south shore is open and hot in August, so go clockwise on hot days to finish in the shade.

The loop is popular with trail runners and mountain bikers. Keep dogs close on the road sections.

Name: Mill Pond Stroll
Summary: A flat, gravel loop around a former mill pond, now a bird reserve. Benches every two hundred metres.
Highlights: Fully accessible|Bird reserve|Benches throughout|Café at the car park
Description:
The pond was built for the sawmill in 1908 and left to the birds when the mill closed. The gravel path around it is level and wide and takes half an hour at a wander.

Herons nest on the island in spring and the hide on the east bank is the place to watch them. The café by the car park opens at nine.

This is the best walk in the guide for a short winter afternoon.

Name: Basin Bluffs
Summary: A loop over the sandstone bluffs south of the reservoir, with arbutus groves and long views down the basin.
Highlights: Sandstone bluffs|Arbutus groves|Views down the basin|Spring flowers
Description:
The loop climbs through Douglas fir onto a series of sandstone bluffs. The rock is rough and grippy when dry and treacherous when wet, and the trail crosses it several times.

Arbutus grows on the bluff tops and the groves are the reason to come. Camas and shooting star flower among them in April.

The bluffs are a sensitive habitat. Stay on the marked route and keep dogs leashed.

Name: Old Railway Grade
Trailhead: Mill Pond car park to Harbour Road
Summary: A flat, straight walk or ride along the abandoned logging railway from the mill pond to the coast.
Highlights: Flat for fifteen kilometres|Two trestle bridges|Shared with cyclists|Ends at the coast
Description:
The railway carried logs from the Lower Basin to the harbour until 1961. The rails are gone and the grade is now a gravel path with a gentle fall toward the sea.

Two trestles cross side valleys and have been redecked with railings. The second is forty metres above the creek and is the highlight.

The grade is shared with cyclists and is straightforward enough to walk in any weather. A bus runs back from Harbour Road twice a day.

Name: Quarry Lake
Summary: A short loop around a flooded quarry with clear green water, cliffs, and a small beach.
Highlights: Clear green water|Swimming beach|Cliff viewpoints|Short and sheltered
Description:
The quarry closed in the 1970s and filled from a spring. The water is clear enough to see the old machinery on the bottom from the cliff viewpoint.

The loop is short and mostly level, with one short climb to the cliffs. The beach at the north end is the local swimming spot.

Do not jump from the cliffs. The water is shallower than it looks in places.

Name: Coastal Bluffs Path
Summary: The signature coast walk of the range, along cliff tops and pocket beaches from the harbour to the cove.
Highlights: Cliff-top views the whole way|Three pocket beaches|Seabird colony in spring|Café at both ends
Description:
The path follows the cliff edge from the harbour breakwater to the cove, dipping to three small beaches along the way. It is never far from the sea and the sound of it.

The seabird colony on the stacks is loudest in May and June. There is a viewpoint with a bench directly opposite.

The path is exposed to wind and there are unfenced drops. It is not a trail for a stormy day.

Name: Lighthouse Point
Summary: An easy walk along the headland to the lighthouse, with a chance of whales in autumn.
Highlights: Working lighthouse|Whale watching in autumn|Mostly level|Shelter at the point
Description:
The path runs along the top of the headland on short grass and reaches the lighthouse in forty minutes. The light still works and the keeper's cottage is a small museum on summer weekends.

Grey whales pass close to the point in October and November. The shelter at the end has a bench and a logbook of sightings.

The headland is open and windy. Bring a layer even in summer.

Name: Smugglers Cove
Summary: A loop down to a hidden cove through a steep gully, returning over the bluff tops.
Highlights: Hidden sandy cove|Steep gully with steps|Sea cave at low tide|Bluff-top return
Description:
The route drops steeply through a wooded gully on timber steps to a sandy cove that is invisible from above. A sea cave at the north end can be entered for an hour either side of low tide.

The return climbs the far side of the cove and follows the bluffs back to the car park with the sea on your left the whole way.

Check the tide before descending. The cove floods at the top of a spring tide.

Name: Estuary Boardwalk
Summary: A level boardwalk across the salt marsh with hides for watching wading birds.
Highlights: Fully accessible|Three bird hides|Salt marsh flowers in summer|Sunrise spot
Description:
The boardwalk crosses the estuary marsh in a wide loop with three hides along the way. It is flat, railed, and open to wheelchairs and pushchairs.

The estuary is the best birdwatching in the range. Waders feed on the mud at low tide and the hides are busiest at dawn in autumn.

The boardwalk can be closed at very high tides. Check the sign at the car park.

Name: Bluff to Basin Link
Trailhead: Cove Lane car park to Bluff Road trailhead
Summary: A long connector from the coast up to the Basin Bluffs, through farmland, forest, and the old quarry workings.
Highlights: Links coast to basin|Old quarry workings|Farm lanes and forest|Few people
Description:
The link leaves the cove and climbs inland through farm lanes and a long stretch of forest to the old quarry workings below the Basin Bluffs. It is a connecting trail rather than a destination, and it is quiet for that reason.

The quarry workings are fenced but the path passes the old crusher and a row of workers' cottages.

This is a long day with a lot of road walking. Combine it with the Basin Bluffs loop for a two-day trip with a night at Bluff Camp.
